thread.title: From The Daily: For change, vote Makled and Schostak for UMich Regent
thread.title_full: From The Daily: For change, vote Makled and Schostak for UMich Regent

author: The Michigan Daily Editorial Board
title: From The Daily: For change, vote Makled and Schostak for UMich Regent
text:
Over the past few years, this Editorial Board’s opinion on the University of Michigan’s Board of Regents has been well documented.
From making repressive changes to the Statement of Student Rights and Responsibilities to hiring a private security company to surveil students , the regents — regardless of party affiliation — have consistently trampled on the liberties of the student body. In times of campus turmoil, instead of working to lead with students in mind, they have taken action to concentrate power.
This Editorial Board was unenthusiastic about the prospects for change ahead of the Michigan Democratic Convention this past March. Jordan Acker and Paul Brown — both members of the current Board — were the presumptive nominees for the Democratic Party in a year where a blue wave seems imminent.
A Guardian investigation shattered this notion after publishing a series of crude and sexually explicit comments sent by Acker in a Slack channel. Several of them were about students. When a University administration-sponsored investigation confirmed the report, his fellow regents chose not to take action. One even called it a “teachable moment” for students. Needless to say, Acker didn’t receive the nomination.
Instead, Democratic delegates chose Brown and Amir Makled as their nominees. Makled is a civil rights attorney from Dearborn, whose campaign has a focus on activism, transparency and student freedom of speech. Brown , a managing partner at ELab Ventures , is a self-proclaimed progressive who has served on the Board for eight years.
At first glance, the two Republican nominees — motor oil magnate Lena Epstein and Bloomfield Township Treasurer Michael Schostak — seem like typical Republican Party candidates. This is a concerning association considering the party’s near-total deference to the whims of President Donald Trump. For Epstein, this appears to hold true. Schostak deviates from this norm.
The moral corruption of the current Board is inadmissible, and this Editorial Board cannot, in good conscience, endorse any incumbent candidates. In fact, we even considered not issuing an endorsement in this race. However, it is abundantly clear that the status quo must end, and the only way out is to elect the candidates that represent the starkest break from current leadership.
While Epstein did not interview with us within our allotted timeframe, conversations with Makled, Brown and Schostak demonstrated that there are only two candidates capable of enacting the change the University needs. So, on Nov. 3, vote Makled and Schostak for University of Michigan regents.
Why Amir Makled
For an overwhelmingly progressive campus, Makled is a more obvious choice for regent. In more ways than one, Makled’s message has been especially resonant with young people. He has committed to pushing back on federal overreach, ensuring free speech protections for students and providing new perspectives to the ideologically homogeneous Board. He is known for frequently appearing on campus and meeting with student groups, and he has even campaigned alongside Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate.
Fundamentally, Makled’s anti-establishment platform is one this Editorial Board can support, and one that would bring a much-needed shakeup to a regency that is increasingly out of touch.
Still, he is far from the perfect candidate. In the lead-up to the Democratic primary, dark money group Michigan Deserves Better released police reports filed against Makled, alleging he abused his wife and nephew. However, these allegations remain unconfirmed by any major news outlet, and his ex-wife has since released a statement denying that abuse occurred.
Additionally, in 2023, he reposted — and has since deleted — a series of harmful tweets many considered to be antisemitic. This behavior is unacceptable and was a large part of this Editorial Board’s deliberation.
However, we have come to the conclusion that Makled is running as a fundamentally different candidate in the general election. When asked about these past posts in an interview with this Editorial Board, Makled affirmed his commitment to Jewish students on campus and condemned hate speech.
“I would totally reject any forms of antisemitic remarks,” Makled said. “I would defend Jewish students, Jewish faculty and Jewish staff as if I was defending my own members of my own family.”
This Editorial Board finds Makled’s past comments disconcerting, but after his interview, we believe he is committed to serving Jewish students. Ultimately, he represents an opportunity to vote for a regent who is open to engaging with all student perspectives.
Why not Paul Brown
It would be easy to say “vote blue no matter who,” but given the failure of the Board to responsibly lead the University and its students, this Editorial Board will not endorse incumbent Paul Brown. As a candidate, Brown attempts to characterize himself as a hyperprogressive friend to students; his tenure would suggest otherwise.
During his time on the Board, the University has faced several public relations crises: Its scandal-ridden University Athletic Department has garnered significant bad press, and the University’s administration provoked backlash in its quest to develop a data center in Ypsilanti Township.
When pressed on some of these issues during an interview with this Editorial Board, Brown was genuinely unaware at best, or at worst, feigned ignorance. At times, his commentary was even alarming — specifically in regard to sexual abuse and reporting failures occurring at the University.
“(The University Athletic Department) is a canary in the coal mine,” Brown said. “What is happening at the Athletic Department is probably not exclusive to the Athletic Department. It is happening at the hospital, and it’s happening in the dorms and in the lecture halls and the professors’ offices on campus.”
The regents perform large-scale oversight of these parts of campus; Brown’s casual resignation to campus-wide dysfunction, coupled with his lack of solutions, implied an indifference toward these institutional problems.
Moreover, Brown recently labeled the University’s choice to establish the data center development in Ypsilanti Township as an act of “ environmental racism ” — one that he voted for. When asked about the development, he spun a convenient narrative; Brown claimed he was uninformed about the siting process and characterized his approval of the property purchase as a “bait and switch.”
In any other position, a blunder of this magnitude would constitute a fireable offense.
While these are very different campus issues, they exemplify the same problem: Brown has historically been complacent in the face of large-scale community concerns, and in his interview he was unable to explain the dissonance between his actions and his rhetoric.
Why Michael Schostak
Given Brown’s failures as regent, this Editorial Board decided to evaluate other candidates for the regency: the Republican nominees. Historically, we have seldom endorsed a Republican, and with the party’s sharp turn toward the far-right, it has felt all-the-more improbable in recent years.
But one Republican candidate assured us he was not subject to the national trend. That is why this Editorial Board has chosen to endorse Michael Schostak for regent — our first Republican endorsement in more than 20 years .
Both Makled and Schostak have platform points aimed at increasing in-state student admission to the University. Additionally, the University’s Go Blue Guarantee is a focus of Schostak’s platform, as he hopes to expand its coverage to include families with higher income thresholds. As it stands, the program covers in-state tuition for households that make less than $125,000 a year. He wants to tweak the policy to exclude assets from the net worth tabulation, which will provide greater access to lower income students.
In an interview with this Editorial Board, Schostak promised to push back on the regents’ inaccessibility.
“I pledge to make myself available. I’ll be visible on campus. I want to learn what’s going on. I want to walk around, talk to people,” Schostak said. “You know, if you just stay up in the ivory tower, you’re really flying blind.”
Along with their growing reclusiveness, the regents have taken concrete steps to curtail free speech, targeting specific viewpoints and imposing concerning limits on students’ right to protest. When asked about free speech concerns, Schostak answered with an attitude that indicated a desire to make the University a home to open debate.
“People feel afraid to speak out — whatever their cause is — for fear of intimidation, retaliation or harassment,” Schostak said. “And I think that that’s wrong and that’s antithetical to what a university experience is supposed to be about.”
Still, Schostak’s Republican affiliation comes with baggage.
In March, The Michigan Daily published a previous version of Schostak’s website that featured troubling policy positions, revealing intentions to bar transgender women from women’s sports and “stop the infiltration” of Chinese international students. These positions were removed from his website that same month.
When pressed on these past positions, Schostak pledged to “fully support and respect the trans population.” Still, he shared his belief that trans women who transitioned post-adolescence should be barred from competition.
In reference to his previous statements about Chinese international students, he said that he does not believe “any group of students is generally untrustworthy,” rather his policy was meant to emphasize his concern for specific incidents that occurred at the University.
Removal and contextualization still aren’t enough, and while Schostak’s sentiment might be sincere, we urge him to amend his position to better reflect the values of the student body.
During his interview, Schostak made it clear that he is a fiscal conservative, and has not bought into Trump’s strand of the Republican Party. For that reason, we are hopeful that he will not thoughtlessly comply with the president’s agenda.
Ultimately, this race is not about partisanship; it is about how candidates will serve students to make life more affordable, protect free speech and value their perspectives.
There is only one way to ensure student concerns will be considered: Vote Amir Makled and Michael Schostak for University of Michigan regents on Nov. 3.
This editorial represents the opinion of The Michigan Daily’s Editorial Board. If you are interested in submitting an Op-Ed or Letter to the Editor, please send your submission to tothedaily@michigandaily.com .
